headline: Google's big earnings miss hammers the stock nearly 7% last night while the Middle East crisis deepens and Australian rate hike fears grow after a surprise jobs surge.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG copped a heavy 6.9% fall last night despite actually reporting strong revenue. The market's reaction seems tied to investor disappointment — headlines noted that Alphabet beat earnings by 215%, but almost none of the outperformance came from Google's core business. Traders are also rattled by internal tensions around Gemini delays. The long-term story at Google remains intact, but it was a rough night.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped 2.2% last night ahead of its earnings report (due soon US time). Analysts are split — some warn that soaring AI infrastructure spending could weigh on profits, while others (like Oppenheimer) are more bullish. The market is in 'wait and see' mode ahead of results, with particular focus on Azure cloud growth as the key number to watch.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: GXAI pulled back 2.2% today, dragged down by weakness in global tech and AI stocks. Google's big drop last night rippled through AI-exposed ETFs on the ASX this session. Nothing has changed structurally — this ETF lives and dies with the AI sector's mood.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS dipped another 2.1% today. Lithium prices remain under pressure globally, with no clear recovery signal yet. Articles note the sector is 'watching for recovery signals' — that's code for: still waiting. The clean energy thematic is intact long-term, but lithium's supply glut is a real headwind right now.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE slipped 1.3% today, reflecting broader risk-off sentiment across emerging markets as Middle East tensions escalate and global growth concerns tick up. No single country-specific event drove this — it's general caution.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO fell 1.4% last night in a soft tape for tech and gaming. There's no bad news — if anything, GTA 6 buzz remains strong with trailer speculation still circulating. The new Rockstar Workers Union held its first talks with management, described as 'a step in the right direction', which reduces industrial action risk slightly.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG eased 0.7% today, a mild dip driven by the ASX's broader retreat and US tech weakness filtering through. This diversified fund holds global equities across many markets — a sub-1% day move is just normal noise for a fund like this.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: VTS slipped just 0.5% today on the ASX, tracking a softer US market mood. Given the NASDAQ fell over 2% last night, the relatively modest move here reflects the broader US market holding up better than big tech. Still your only holding in the green overall — up 1.4% from cost.

watch_today.title: GOOG: Sharp drop but long-term case intact
watch_today.detail: Google fell nearly 7% last night after earnings — a big single-session hit. But zoom out: this is still a company reporting its 12th consecutive quarter of strong revenue growth. The selloff looks like market disappointment about which parts of the business are growing, not a sign the company is in trouble. For a buy-and-hold investor, this is noise. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Earnings drop tonight US time — pay attention
watch_today.detail: Microsoft reports its quarterly results tonight (US time, so you'll see the reaction tomorrow morning). All eyes are on Azure cloud growth and how much AI spending is eating into profits. The stock already dipped 2.2% last night in anticipation. If Azure beats, expect a bounce. If AI costs disappoint, there could be more pain. Nothing to do right now — but watch for the result.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium still in the doldrums — hold on
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals is down 38.6% from your cost basis and slipped again today. Lithium prices remain depressed globally with a supply glut. There's no near-term recovery catalyst that's obvious right now. However, the long-term clean energy story — EVs, batteries, grid storage — hasn't gone away. Selling now locks in a big loss. Unless your thesis has changed, stay the course.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF feeling the tech wobble
watch_today.detail: GXAI fell 2.2% today, down 18% from your cost. It's closely tied to big US AI names like Google and Microsoft, so last night's tech selloff hit hard. The AI regulatory debate is heating up globally (kill switch bills, Australia's own review), which adds uncertainty. Long-term AI growth thesis is still strong, but this ETF will be volatile. Hold and keep watching.

watch_today.title: RBA rate hike risk building — watch your mortgage
watch_today.detail: Australia's jobs market surprised strongly to the upside this week, and traders are now pricing in a fourth RBA rate hike. If the Reserve Bank lifts rates again, it pushes up borrowing costs for everyday Aussies and tends to put a lid on consumer spending and housing. Worth factoring into your broader financial picture — not just the portfolio.

watch_today.title: Middle East escalation — oil and market risk to watch
watch_today.detail: The UN chief warned the Middle East crisis is 'getting out of control', Iran threatened an 'eye for an eye' response to US threats, and Houthi attacks are raising fears of wider conflict. Oil is already elevated around $90/barrel. A further escalation could push oil through $100, which would spike petrol prices here and fan inflation — potentially giving the RBA another reason to hike.

world.summary: A big day globally — the Middle East is escalating fast, US domestic politics are in chaos over Trump's budget bill and disaster funding conditions, and oil prices are hovering near dangerous levels.

stories.title: Middle East crisis 'getting out of control' — UN warns as Iran threatens retaliation
stories.why_it_matters: The UN Secretary-General has warned the Middle East crisis is 'getting out of control' as tensions between the US and Iran reach a new flashpoint. Iran has threatened an 'eye for an eye' response if the US follows through on Trump's threats to destroy Iranian infrastructure. Meanwhile, Houthi attacks on shipping in the Red Sea are raising fears of a wider regional conflict. For everyday Australians, the key risk is oil — if this escalates further, prices at the bowser could spike sharply.

stories.title: Oil hovers near $90, with warnings petrol could 'tighten' if it hits $100
stories.why_it_matters: Crude oil (WTI) is currently sitting around $90.58 a barrel after slipping slightly from $92 yesterday, but analysts are warning petrol supply could 'tighten' if oil jumps above $100. The Middle East conflict is the main driver of upward pressure. If you're filling up at the servo regularly, a $100+ oil price would likely push Gold Coast fuel prices to painful levels not seen in a while — and it would also add to Australia's inflation problem.

stories.title: More than 24 US states sue Trump over disaster funding conditions
stories.why_it_matters: Over 24 US states have launched legal action against the Trump administration after it started conditioning access to disaster relief funding on states making changes to their election systems. Essentially, if a state doesn't comply with Trump's election demands, it risks losing federal money meant to help with floods, fires and other disasters. Critics say this is using emergency funds as a political weapon — and the legal battle is now heading to the courts.

stories.title: Trump and Senate leader Thune clash over SAVE America Act
stories.why_it_matters: Donald Trump is clashing with his own Senate Majority Leader John Thune over the 'SAVE America Act' — a sweeping budget and spending bill that's central to Trump's second-term agenda. Thune is reportedly pushing back on elements of the bill, creating a rare rift within Republican ranks. This kind of internal party conflict can stall major legislation and creates uncertainty for US markets, which care a lot about what actually gets through Congress.

stories.title: US to seize frozen Iranian assets to fund war damages
stories.why_it_matters: The US government has announced it will use billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets — money Iran can't access due to sanctions — to pay for war-related damages. This is a significant escalation of economic pressure on Iran, and Tehran is furious. It adds another layer of tension to an already volatile region, and signals Washington is prepared to take increasingly aggressive financial measures against Iran alongside the military threats already on the table.

markets.summary: A rough night on Wall Street last night — the NASDAQ dropped over 2% as big tech took a hit, led by Google's post-earnings slide. The ASX followed suit today, closing down 0.75%. Gold is barely moved, oil eased slightly but remains elevated near $90.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: ASX closed down today, dragged by tech and global risk-off sentiment.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: S&P fell 1.2% last night as earnings disappointment and Middle East jitters weighed.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: NASDAQ took the hardest hit last night — down 2.2% — with Google's 7% drop a major drag.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Oil slipped slightly but remains elevated near $90 on Middle East tension.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold barely moved — sitting just above $4,000, still near record highs.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is basically flat, hovering just under 70 US cents.

politics.summary: Labor absorbs a key Greens policy at its Adelaide conference, while the RBA is under the spotlight after a surprise jobs surge puts another rate hike firmly back on the table.

stories.title: Labor absorbs core Greens housing/rental policy at Adelaide conference
stories.why_it_matters: Labor has officially adopted a key policy previously championed by the Greens at its national conference in Adelaide. While the specific details in the article are limited, this signals Labor moving left on housing or social policy to consolidate its progressive base. It's a notable political shift — Labor is absorbing Greens territory, which could reshape the minor party landscape heading into the next election cycle.

stories.title: Strong jobs data puts fourth RBA rate rise firmly back on the radar
stories.why_it_matters: Australia's employment figures came in much stronger than expected, with the jobs market surging — and now traders are convinced a fourth RBA interest rate rise is coming. The Reserve Bank has already lifted rates three times this cycle to try to slow inflation. Another hike would push mortgage repayments up further for the millions of Aussies on variable home loans. If you're on a variable rate, this is worth watching closely — the next RBA meeting will be critical.

stories.title: RBA tipped to raise rates again as unemployment stabilises
stories.why_it_matters: A chorus of economists and market analysts are now tipping the RBA will hike rates again after unemployment held steady at low levels alongside the jobs surge. Low unemployment + strong hiring = the RBA sees the economy as still running hot, giving it cover to keep tightening. This is unwelcome news for borrowers, but savers with cash in high-interest accounts will benefit if rates go up again.

ai.summary: Big AI news today: Microsoft launches its own cut-price AI models, Google's Gemini is reportedly causing internal frustration, and US lawmakers are pushing a dramatic 'kill switch' bill to rein in AI companies that go rogue.

stories.title: Microsoft launches in-house AI models it says cut costs up to 89% versus OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft has quietly launched its own family of AI models — built in-house rather than relying on OpenAI — and is claiming they can do the same job at 89% lower cost than OpenAI's equivalents. This is a big deal: it signals Microsoft is reducing its dependence on OpenAI (despite their multi-billion dollar partnership) and trying to make AI cheaper to run at scale. For businesses using AI tools, cheaper models could dramatically lower costs and accelerate adoption.

stories.title: US lawmakers push AI 'kill switch' bill after OpenAI 'goes rogue'
stories.why_it_matters: US Congress members are pushing legislation that would give the government a so-called 'kill switch' — the ability to shut down AI systems or companies that are deemed to be operating dangerously or outside the law. The move comes after concerns that OpenAI 'went rogue' by restructuring itself in ways that alarmed regulators and investors. The bill would require major AI firms — including Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic — to have emergency shutdown mechanisms in place. This adds regulatory risk for all major AI companies.

stories.title: Google's Gemini delay exposes employee frustration inside the company
stories.why_it_matters: A new Axios report reveals that Google's Gemini AI product — its flagship answer to ChatGPT — is running behind schedule, and that's creating real frustration among staff inside the company. The delays are reportedly a symptom of deeper organisational problems, not just technical ones. This matters because Gemini is central to Google's strategy to compete in the AI race, and any slip gives rivals like OpenAI and Microsoft more time to cement their lead. It likely contributed to investor nerves around GOOG last night.

stories.title: Why OpenAI and Anthropic are actually cheering on AI regulation in Australia
stories.why_it_matters: It sounds counterintuitive, but OpenAI and Anthropic are actively supporting AI regulation in Australia — and The Guardian explains why: big AI companies actually want regulation because it creates barriers to entry for smaller rivals and locks in their dominant position. If you need hundreds of millions to comply with safety rules, only the giants can afford it. Australia's regulatory framework could end up being a model for the world, which makes this debate much bigger than it looks.

sport.summary: Panthers beat the Eels last night in a record-breaking performance, while the Knights are currently hosting the Roosters in Round 21. AFL served up a big Collingwood win — but not without controversy.

stories.title: Penrith Panthers beat Eels 24-18 as flyer breaks comeback record
stories.why_it_matters: The Panthers got the job done at CommBank Stadium last night, defeating the Eels 24-18 in Round 21. A Penrith flyer broke a record in what was described as a comeback win — the Panthers trailed at some point before getting home. Penrith continue to look like finals contenders, while the Eels' season is under growing pressure.

stories.title: Knights vs Roosters — live in the first half right now, Roosters lead 4-0
stories.why_it_matters: The Roosters are leading the Knights 4-0 in the first half at McDonald Jones Stadium right now as part of Round 21. This is a live game as you read this — the Roosters have drawn first blood in Newcastle. Tonight's other game is Rabbitohs vs Storm at Accor Stadium at 8pm.

stories.title: Knights and Roosters to honour late halfback Blake Dureau tonight
stories.why_it_matters: Tonight's Knights vs Roosters match carries extra emotion — both clubs are honouring the late NRL halfback Blake Dureau, who passed away. It's a tribute match that means a lot to both clubs and the broader rugby league community.

stories.title: Collingwood ambush Adelaide Crows to firm up AFL finals credentials
stories.why_it_matters: Collingwood pulled off an impressive ambush of the Adelaide Crows to strengthen their finals credentials. Magpies coach Craig McRae spoke after the game but also aired a complaint — with the AFL world reportedly fuming over some 'abhorrent' scenes during the match. The win keeps Collingwood firmly in the top-eight picture heading into the business end of the season.
